name: Pelvic Inflammatory Disease
preview_text: The type of pelvic pain - burning and throbbing versus cold and heavy - reveals a completely different internal imbalance. Treating that imbalance can not only relieve pain but als...
synonyms: ["PID", "Acute pelvic inflammatory disease", "Acute Pelvic Inflammatory", "Abrupt Inflammation Of The Pelvis", "Acute Pelvic Infection", "Sudden Pelvic Inflammation"]
conventional_description:
Pelvic inflammatory disease is an infection of the female reproductive organs - the uterus, fallopian tubes, and ovaries. It is most often caused by sexually transmitted bacteria, such as chlamydia and gonorrhea, that travel upward from the vagina. Typical symptoms include lower abdominal pain, abnormal vaginal discharge, fever, painful urination, and pain during intercourse.
Diagnosis usually involves a pelvic exam, swabs to test for infection, and sometimes an ultrasound to check for abscesses or inflammation. Even after the infection is cleared with antibiotics, many women are left with chronic pelvic pain, scar tissue, and a higher risk of infertility or ectopic pregnancy.
conventional_treatments: Antibiotics are the cornerstone of conventional treatment, often given as a combination to cover multiple bacteria. Severe cases may require intravenous antibiotics and hospitalization. Pain relievers are used for discomfort, and surgery may be needed to drain an abscess or remove adhesions in chronic cases. While antibiotics effectively clear the acute infection, they do not address the lingering pelvic congestion, pain, or constitutional weakness that can make recurrent infections more likely.
tcm_understanding:
TCM sees the pelvic cavity as part of the Lower Burner, a region governed by the Liver, Kidneys, and the extraordinary Chong and Ren vessels. These channels are responsible for the smooth flow of Qi and Blood through the uterus and ovaries. When they become blocked or weakened, pain and inflammation follow. The most common culprits are Damp-Heat (a combination of infection and inflammation) and Qi stagnation (often from emotional stress), both of which lead to Blood stasis - the central mechanism behind chronic pelvic pain.
Blood stasis is the common thread that ties all PID patterns together. Imagine a river that slows down and becomes murky; in the pelvis, this means thick, sluggish blood that causes fixed, stabbing pain, dark clots, and adhesions.
What creates that stagnation varies. In some women, Damp-Heat from an acute infection congeals the blood. In others, emotional frustration knots the Liver Qi, preventing it from pushing blood smoothly. In still others, a constitutional weakness of Qi or Yang fails to warm and circulate, allowing Cold-Dampness to settle deep in the pelvis.
This is why two women with the same Western diagnosis of PID can have completely different symptom pictures. One may have a burning pain, yellow discharge, and a rapid pulse, while another feels a cold, heavy ache with clear white discharge and a slow, weak pulse. TCM treats each of these as a different pattern, using herbs and acupuncture that match the specific internal climate - clearing Heat, warming Cold, moving Qi, or nourishing deficiency - rather than a one-size-fits-all antibiotic.
classical_quote: 「夫带下俱是湿症。而以带名者，因带脉不能约束而有此病，故以名之。... 脾气之虚，肝气之郁，湿气之侵，热气之逼，安得不成带下之病哉！」
classical_translation: "All leukorrhea disorders are dampness patterns. It is named after the Dai (Girdle) vessel because the vessel fails to restrain and thus the illness arises. ... With Spleen qi deficiency, Liver qi depression, dampness invasion, and heat pressing, how could leukorrhea not develop? This captures the TCM understanding that pelvic discharge and pain arise from a combination of dampness, heat, stagnation, and deficiency - the very roots of pelvic inflammatory disease."
classical_source:
Fu Qing Zhu Nu Ke (傅青主女科)  ,  Chapter on Leukorrhea (带下) 									·

tcm_diagnosis:
To work out which pattern is driving pelvic inflammatory disease (盆腔炎, pén qiāng yán), a practitioner listens carefully to how the pain actually feels. A sharp, burning ache that feels hot points in one direction, while a dull, heavy coldness points in another. The colour, texture and smell of vaginal discharge are just as important, and the tongue and pulse are checked to confirm the internal picture.
When damp-heat and toxic heat settle deep in the pelvis, the result is Heat and Blood Stagnation in the Lower Burner. The pain feels hot and throbbing, often with a thick yellow or pus-like discharge that may have an unpleasant odour. The tongue is red with a greasy yellow coating, and the pulse is rapid and slippery - signs of heat and dampness trapped together.
If emotional stress or surgery has disrupted the smooth flow of Qi, Qi and Blood Stagnation takes hold. The pain is fixed and stabbing, and the lower abdomen often feels distended. Periods may become irregular with dark clots. Here the tongue looks dusky or purple, and the pulse feels wiry - like a tight guitar string - reflecting the stuck, tense quality of the Qi.
A completely different picture appears with Cold-Dampness in the Lower Burner. The pain is a heavy, cold ache that gets worse with chilly weather or long periods of sitting, and the discharge is thick and white. The tongue is pale and swollen with a white greasy coat, while the pulse is deep and slow - signs of cold congealing the blood and dampness weighing everything down.

patterns.pattern_name: Heat and Blood Stagnation in the Lower Burner
patterns.symptoms: ["Fixed, stabbing pelvic pain", "Sensation of heat in the pelvis", "Dark menstrual blood with clots", "Yellow, sticky vaginal discharge", "Irritability and emotional tension"]
patterns.worse_with: Spicy, fried, or heating foods, Alcohol, Emotional stress, Cold or damp environments, Overwork or overexertion
patterns.better_with: Applying warmth to the lower abdomen, Rest, Cooling foods, Stress reduction, Gentle movement or exercise
patterns.why_this_happens: When heat accumulates in the pelvic cavity, it can dry up fluids and make the blood thick and sluggish. This stagnant blood then blocks the channels, causing a fixed, stabbing pain in the lower abdomen. The heat also disturbs the mind, leading to restlessness and irritability, and often produces a yellow, sticky vaginal discharge.
patterns.tongue_and_pulse: Tongue: reddish-purple body with stasis spots, distended sublingual veins, and a dry yellow coating. Pulse: deep, choppy (Se), and rapid (Shu).
patterns.why_triggers_reliefs_work: Heat and stagnant blood are the root of this pain. Spicy foods and stress add more heat and stagnation, while cold environments congeal the blood further. Gentle warmth helps move blood without overheating, and cooling foods clear heat. Rest and stress reduction calm the mind, allowing qi to flow and stasis to resolve.
patterns.diet_and_lifestyle: Avoid spicy, greasy foods and alcohol, which add heat. Eat cooling, blood-moving foods like celery, mung beans, and hawthorn. Gentle daily walking helps blood circulation, but avoid overexertion. Keep the lower abdomen comfortably warm without overheating.

patterns.why_this_happens: Emotional stress, frustration, or unresolved anger disrupts the Liver's ability to keep Qi moving smoothly. When Qi stagnates in the pelvic region, it can no longer propel Blood through the vessels, leading to Blood stasis. This stagnation produces a fixed, stabbing pain in the lower abdomen, often accompanied by a bloating or distending sensation. The impaired circulation also affects the uterus, causing dark, clotted menstrual blood and irregular cycles.
patterns.tongue_and_pulse: Tongue: dark purple body with stasis spots, distended sublingual veins, thin white coat. Pulse: wiry (弦) and choppy (涩), like a taut guitar string scraping bamboo.
patterns.why_triggers_reliefs_work: Emotional stress causes Liver Qi to stagnate, which is the root of this pattern; when Qi doesn't move, Blood stagnates and creates pain. Gentle movement and abdominal massage help unblock Qi and Blood flow. Cold constricts and congeals Blood, worsening stasis, so warmth and warm foods encourage circulation and ease pain.
patterns.diet_and_lifestyle: Incorporate gentle daily movement like walking or yoga to keep Qi flowing; avoid prolonged sitting. Manage stress with meditation or deep breathing, as emotional tension directly worsens stagnation. Eat warming, cooked foods and avoid excessive cold or raw items that can congeal Blood. A warm compress on the lower abdomen can provide temporary relief.

patterns.why_this_happens: Cold and dampness are external pathogens that invade the lower burner when the body's yang qi is weak, often after exposure to cold or damp environments. They congeal in the uterus and channels, blocking the smooth flow of qi and blood. This produces a heavy, cold pain in the lower abdomen, a profuse white watery discharge, and a dragging sensation that worsens with cold or prolonged sitting.
patterns.tongue_and_pulse: Tongue: pale, swollen body with teeth marks, thick white greasy coating, excessively moist. Pulse: deep, slow, and soggy.
patterns.why_triggers_reliefs_work: Cold and dampness are the core pathogens in this pattern. External cold and damp weather, cold foods, and prolonged sitting all increase cold and damp in the lower burner, congealing blood and worsening pain. Warmth, warm foods, and gentle movement help disperse cold, dry dampness, and promote the free flow of qi and blood, directly counteracting the root cause of the discomfort.
patterns.diet_and_lifestyle: Eat warm, cooked foods like soups, stews, and congees. Add warming spices such as ginger, cinnamon, and black pepper. Strictly avoid iced drinks, raw salads, and greasy dairy. Keep the lower abdomen warm with a hot water bottle or moxibustion, and avoid sitting on cold surfaces. Gentle daily walking helps circulate yang qi and dispel dampness.

patterns.symptoms: ["Dull, persistent pelvic ache that worsens with pressure or exertion", "Deep fatigue and lack of strength", "Pale or dusky complexion with a greyish tinge", "Shortness of breath with minimal activity", "Pain is fixed and does not move"]
patterns.worse_with: Overwork or overexertion, Prolonged sitting or standing, Cold or raw foods and iced drinks, Emotional stress
patterns.better_with: Gentle movement or exercise, Applying warmth to the lower abdomen, Rest, Warm, nourishing foods and soups
patterns.why_this_happens: Qi is the vital force that propels blood through the vessels. When Qi is weakened by chronic illness, overwork, or poor nutrition, it lacks the strength to keep blood moving smoothly in the pelvic basin. Circulation slows, and blood begins to pool and stagnate, producing a dull, persistent ache that feels deep and heavy rather than sharp. This stagnation also disrupts the nourishment of the uterus and surrounding tissues, leading to the fatigue, pale complexion, and menstrual irregularities typical of this pattern.
patterns.tongue_and_pulse: Tongue: pale-dark or pale-purple body, possible stasis spots and teeth marks, thin white coat. Pulse: deep, fine, and choppy (rough, hesitant).
patterns.why_triggers_reliefs_work: In Qi deficiency with blood stasis, the body's engine is too weak to push blood through the pelvic vessels. Overexertion and prolonged standing drain the little Qi that remains, causing blood to sludge and pain to worsen. Cold foods and drinks contract the channels, making it even harder for sluggish blood to move. Gentle movement, on the other hand, stimulates Qi flow without depleting it, while warmth relaxes the vessels and encourages circulation. Rest and nourishing warm foods rebuild the Qi reserves needed to break the cycle of stagnation.
patterns.diet_and_lifestyle: Focus on gentle, consistent movement like walking or tai chi to encourage Qi and blood flow without exhausting yourself. Eat warm, easily digestible foods such as congee with red dates, goji berries, and a little ginger; these gently strengthen the Spleen and build Qi. Avoid cold, raw foods and icy drinks, which chill the channels and further slow circulation. Prioritize rest and avoid overwork-your body needs to conserve Qi to heal.

patterns.pattern_name: Blood Stagnation in the Directing and Penetrating Vessels
patterns.symptoms: ["Fixed, stabbing pelvic pain", "Dark menstrual blood with clots", "Painful periods that improve after passing clots", "Pain worsens at night", "Palpable masses or lumps in the lower abdomen", "Difficulty conceiving or infertility"]
patterns.worse_with: Cold or damp environments, Emotional stress, Cold or raw foods and iced drinks, Prolonged sitting or standing, Overwork or overexertion
patterns.better_with: Applying warmth to the lower abdomen, Rest, Passing menstrual clots, Warm, nourishing foods and soups, Gentle movement or exercise
patterns.why_this_happens: When chronic illness or overwork depletes the Kidneys, the Directing and Penetrating Vessels (Chong and Ren) lose their nourishment. Without this vital support, blood flow in the pelvic cavity becomes sluggish and eventually stagnates. This stuck blood lodges in the uterus and surrounding tissues, creating the fixed, stabbing pain, dark clotted menses, and palpable masses typical of chronic pelvic inflammatory disease.
patterns.tongue_and_pulse: Tongue: dark purple body with possible stasis spots, engorged sublingual veins, thin white coat. Pulse: choppy (rough, uneven), often wiry at the left middle position, deep at the rear positions.
patterns.why_triggers_reliefs_work: Cold congeals blood, making stasis worse, so warmth and heat ease pain. Rest conserves Qi, while gentle movement promotes circulation without exhausting the body. Passing clots directly relieves the obstruction. Emotional stress constrains Liver Qi, which further impairs blood flow, so managing stress is essential.
patterns.diet_and_lifestyle: Eat warming, blood-nourishing foods like lamb, ginger, and dark leafy greens. Avoid raw, cold foods and iced drinks. Gentle daily movement such as walking or yoga helps Qi and blood flow. Keep the lower abdomen warm with a hot water bottle, especially during menstruation.

patterns.pattern_name: Kidney and Liver Yin Deficiency causing Heat in the Blood
patterns.symptoms: ["Dull, burning pelvic pain, worse at night", "Night sweats and afternoon tidal heat", "Dry mouth and throat, especially at night", "Thin, dark menstrual blood or spotting", "Low back soreness and weak knees", "Dizziness, ringing in the ears, or dry eyes"]
patterns.worse_with: Overwork or overexertion, Spicy, fried, or heating foods, Emotional stress, Hot weather or overheating
patterns.better_with: Rest, Hydrating fluids and moist foods, Gentle movement or exercise
patterns.why_this_happens: Kidney and Liver Yin are like the body's cooling and nourishing reserves. When chronic inflammation or overwork depletes these reserves, a dry, restless heat builds up deep inside. This "empty heat" rises and disturbs the blood in the pelvic region, causing a low-grade, lingering ache, dark and scant menstrual flow, and a feeling of warmth that worsens at night.
patterns.tongue_and_pulse: Tongue: red, thin, and dry with little or no coating; possible cracks and redder sides. Pulse: fine, rapid, and often wiry at the left middle position, weak at the left rear position.
patterns.why_triggers_reliefs_work: This pattern is driven by a deep deficit of cooling, moistening Yin energy, which allows a dry, restless heat to flare up. Overwork and late nights directly consume the Kidney and Liver Yin, while spicy and heating foods add fuel to the internal fire, worsening pelvic heat and pain. Rest, cooling foods, and hydration help rebuild Yin and gently settle the empty heat, while stress management prevents Liver Qi from stagnating and generating more heat.
patterns.diet_and_lifestyle: Prioritize rest and avoid staying up late, which further drains Yin. Eat cooling, moistening foods like pear, tofu, black sesame, and mung beans, while strictly avoiding spicy, fried, or overly heating foods and alcohol. Gentle, restorative exercises like yoga or tai chi can help, but intense sweating workouts should be limited.

It is especially suited for people who are prone to sweating, tire easily, and experience worsening symptoms in cold or windy conditions. Modern practitioners commonly apply it for peripheral neuropathy, post-stroke numbness, and Raynaud's phenomenon.

formulas.description: A classical formula designed to deeply nourish Kidney Yin and replenish the body's vital essence and marrow. It is used when there is significant depletion of the body's fundamental nourishing fluids and substances, leading to symptoms such as dizziness, lower back and knee weakness, night sweats, dry mouth and throat, and a general state of thinning or exhaustion. Unlike milder Yin-nourishing formulas, Zuo Gui Wan is a purely replenishing formula without any draining ingredients, making it suitable for more severe deficiency.

It builds on the famous Liu Wei Di Huang Wan (Six Ingredient Rehmannia Pill) with two additional cooling herbs.

faqs.question: Can TCM treat pelvic inflammatory disease without antibiotics?
faqs.answer: For an active, acute infection with fever and severe pain, antibiotics are the first line of defense and should not be delayed. TCM can be used alongside antibiotics to reduce inflammation and support recovery. For chronic PID, where the infection has cleared but pain and discharge persist, TCM can be the primary treatment, focusing on resolving blood stasis and dampness that antibiotics cannot address.

faqs.question: How long does it take to see results with acupuncture for PID?
faqs.answer: Many women notice a reduction in pain and a lighter, less bothersome discharge after 3-4 weekly acupuncture sessions. However, lasting change - especially when adhesions or long-standing stasis are involved - typically requires 8-12 weeks of consistent treatment. Acupuncture works by improving local blood flow and calming the nervous system, and its effects build over time.

faqs.question: Is acupuncture safe during an active pelvic infection?
faqs.answer: Acupuncture can be safe and helpful during a mild flare, but if you have a high fever or are acutely unwell, rest and medical care take priority. Always tell your acupuncturist if you suspect an active infection. They may use points away from the abdomen or choose gentler techniques until the acute phase passes.

faqs.question: Can TCM help with fertility after PID?
faqs.answer: Yes. PID can cause scar tissue and blockages in the fallopian tubes, which in TCM terms is severe Blood stasis in the Chong and Ren vessels. Herbs and acupuncture that move blood, reduce inflammation, and nourish the Kidney essence can improve tubal function and the uterine lining. Many women are able to conceive naturally after a course of treatment, though the timeline depends on the extent of damage.

faqs.question: What foods should I avoid with pelvic inflammatory disease?
faqs.answer: Generally, avoid cold, raw foods and icy drinks, which can congeal blood and worsen pain. Greasy, fried, and sugary foods create Dampness, feeding the inflammatory environment. If your pattern involves Heat, also reduce spicy foods and alcohol. Warm, cooked meals - soups, stews, and lightly steamed vegetables - are your best foundation.

faqs.question: Will I need to take herbs every day?
faqs.answer: Most herbal treatment for PID involves a daily decoction or concentrated powder taken in divided doses. This consistent exposure is important to gradually break down blood stasis and shift the underlying pattern. Some formulas are taken only during the menstrual phase to encourage smooth flow and clear clots. Your practitioner will tailor the schedule to your cycle and pattern.

faqs.question: Can TCM help with chronic pelvic pain from adhesions?
faqs.answer: Adhesions are a form of stubborn Blood stasis and often also involve Phlegm. Acupuncture, moxibustion, and blood-moving herbal formulas can soften and reduce adhesions over time, easing the pulling and stabbing pain. External therapies like herbal enemas or warm compresses over the lower abdomen are often added to deliver medicine directly to the pelvic tissues.

faqs.question: Is it safe to combine TCM with my antibiotic treatment?
faqs.answer: In most cases, yes. TCM herbs and acupuncture can complement antibiotics by reducing side effects, supporting the immune system, and addressing the underlying stasis. Always inform both your TCM practitioner and your doctor about all medications and supplements you are taking. Some blood-moving herbs may interact with anticoagulants, so full disclosure is essential.

research.title: Cai's Gynecology Chronic Pelvic Formula for chronic pelvic inflammatory disease: a randomized controlled trial
research.description: This RCT evaluated the efficacy of Cai's Gynecology Chronic Pelvic Formula, a classical TCM prescription containing Chuān Liàn Zǐ, Bài Jiàng Cǎo, Dà Xuè Téng, and Fú Líng, among other herbs. Patients with chronic PID receiving the formula showed significant reductions in pelvic pain scores and serum inflammatory markers compared to the control group, with no serious adverse events reported. The study supports the formula’s role in regulating qi and blood, dispelling dampness, and reducing pelvic inflammation.
research.periodical: Cai X, et al. Am J Transl Res. 2025;17(7):4470-4482.

research.title: Acupuncture combined with heat-sensitive moxibustion for chronic pelvic inflammatory disease: an observation of therapeutic effect
research.description: This clinical study observed the effects of acupuncture at core points such as Guānyuán REN-4, Zǐgōng EX-CA1, and Sānyīnjiāo SP-6, combined with heat-sensitive moxibustion on the lower abdomen, in women with chronic PID. The combined therapy group achieved a significantly higher total effective rate than the acupuncture-only group, with marked improvements in lower abdominal pain, abnormal discharge, and menstrual irregularities. The findings highlight the added benefit of moxibustion in warming the channels and dispersing cold-dampness or stagnant blood.
research.periodical: Zhang Y, et al. Chinese Acupuncture & Moxibustion. 2021;41(9):955-959.

research.title: Data mining analysis of acupoint selection patterns in modern acupuncture treatment for chronic pelvic inflammatory disease
research.description: This data mining study analysed the acupoint prescriptions from a large number of clinical acupuncture trials for chronic PID. The results identified Guānyuán REN-4, Sānyīnjiāo SP-6, Zǐgōng EX-CA1, Zhōngjí REN-3, and Zúsānlǐ ST-36 as the core acupoints, with variations according to pattern differentiation. The study provides an evidence-based framework for standardised acupuncture protocols in PID treatment and confirms the central role of the Ren and Spleen channels.
research.periodical: Li J, et al. Acupuncture Research. 2021;46(8):704-710.
